opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it came from reading older papers rather than only the newest ones.

The starting point was linear attention. When you write it out, linear attention is basically an RNN with a matrix-valued hidden state: at each step you add an outer product of key and value into that state. It's purely additive. You keep writing into memory and never erase anything, so with a finite state, retrieval gets noisy and recall-intensive tasks suffer.

Then I read the fast weight programmer line of work, especially the paper by Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie, and Jürgen Schmidhuber showing that linear transformers are essentially fast weight programmers. They proposed replacing the additive update with the delta rule. That idea goes back to the Widrow-Hoff rule. Before writing a new value for a key, you first read out what the memory currently associates with that key and correct it toward the target. So the memory can overwrite and fix itself instead of just piling things up. That felt like the right inductive bias, and it connects nicely to the view of the recurrent state as online regression, or test-time learning.

The problem was that their version was trained sequentially, step by step, so it couldn't use modern hardware well and didn't scale. That's where I think my background helped. Earlier I had worked on chunkwise parallel training for gated linear attention, and I'd been reading systems and hardware-efficient algorithm papers, like the FlashAttention line, which made me think in terms of tensor cores, I/O, and chunking rather than just FLOPs.

The key realization came from looking at the structure of the delta rule update. Each step multiplies the state by an identity-minus-rank-one matrix, which is a generalized Householder transformation. Once you see that, you can go back to classical numerical linear algebra. There's the WY representation from the 1980s, which compactly represents products of Householder matrices. Using that, you can compute the products within a chunk in parallel with mostly matrix multiplications, and only pass a recurrent state between chunks. That made DeltaNet trainable at scale.

So I'd say my approach was a mix of three threads. Linear attention gave me the framework. The fast weight literature gave me the right update rule. Old numerical linear algebra gave me the tool to make it efficient. A lot of good ideas are already sitting in older papers, and sometimes the contribution is noticing that a decades-old technique solves a modern bottleneck. That lesson also carried into later work like Gated DeltaNet, where we combined the delta rule with gating, inspired by Mamba2's decay, so the model can both precisely edit memory and quickly forget.

fable-5.1.text:
When I started on this line of work, I actually went back quite far, not just to the recent linear attention papers but to the older literature on fast weights and associative memory. The delta rule itself goes back to Widrow-Hoff in the 1960s, and Schmidhuber's fast weight programmer work from the early 90s already had the idea that one network could write into the weights of another. Then in 2021 the Schlag, Irie, and Schmidhuber paper connected that explicitly to linear transformers and proposed DeltaNet as an update rule. So the core idea was not mine. What struck me when reading those papers was that the idea was correct but nobody had made it run fast on modern hardware.

Reading the linear attention line, from Katharopoulos onward, and then RetNet, Mamba, GLA, I started to see them all through one lens. They are all recurrent state updates on a matrix-valued memory, and the differences come down to how you write into that memory and how you forget. Linear attention is a pure additive outer product update, which means the memory just accumulates and keys collide. Gated variants add decay, which helps with forgetting but still cannot do targeted overwriting. The delta rule is different because it first reads out what is currently stored for a key, computes an error, and only writes the correction. That is a much more expressive memory operation, and it explains why DeltaNet does so much better on things like associative recall.

The thing that shaped the engineering side was understanding why DeltaNet had been neglected. The update is sequentially dependent in a way the additive rule is not, so you cannot trivially use the chunkwise parallel form that made GLA and others trainable at scale. So my approach became, take an old idea that people had evaluated at small scale and dismissed, and figure out the right reparameterization so that it fits the chunked matmul structure that tensor cores want. Once we found the WY representation trick for the product of Householder-like updates, the whole thing became hardware efficient, and then it was mostly a matter of scaling and seeing whether the theoretical advantages held up. They did.

So I would say reading the history gave me two things. Humility, because most of the ideas already exist, and a sense of where the actual gap was, which was not conceptual but computational.

astra-6.text:
Reading earlier architecture papers helped me think about what a model’s state is actually doing. Rather than just asking how to make attention more efficient, I started asking: what information is being stored, and how should that information be updated?

One idea that stood out was to view the state as an associative memory. With an additive update, you keep putting information into that memory, but it’s harder to revise an association that’s already there. The delta rule gives you a way to do that: retrieve what the memory currently predicts, compare it with what you want to store, and update based on the error.

That perspective shaped how I approached DeltaNet. The update rule and the efficient implementation had to be considered together. An appealing memory mechanism is only part of the story; you also need to make it practical to train.

sol-6.1.text:
Reading those earlier papers helped me think about linear attention as a memory system. You write information into a fixed-size state, and then you retrieve it with a query. From that perspective, the important question becomes: what is the right rule for updating that memory?

With the usual additive update, you keep adding key–value associations, but it’s difficult to correct something already stored. The delta rule gives you a different approach: first look at what the memory currently predicts for a key, then update it using the difference between that prediction and the value you want to store.

That connection to earlier work on fast weights and associative memory really shaped our approach to DeltaNet. It suggested that we could improve the memory update itself, while the practical challenge was making that update efficient enough to train on modern hardware.
